title: H-1B in 2026: Seven Pressures Reshaping the U.S. Skilled-Visa Pipeline
excerpt: A $100,000 offshore fee, a wage-weighted lottery and a proposed end to the 60-day grace period have made 2026 the hardest year in recent memory for America's flagship skilled-worker visa.
body:
• A $100,000 fee on H-1B petitions filed from outside the US and a new wage-weighted lottery have collapsed demand: USCIS received 358,737 FY2026 registrations, down 25% year-on-year and the fewest since FY2022.
  • A rule published September 11 would scrap the 60-day grace period for laid-off H-1B, L-1, O-1 and TN workers, pushing them out of status the day after their job ends.
  • Approval rates hold near 98%, but heavier documentation demands, site visits and "catch-and-revoke" enforcement have sharply raised compliance costs for employers.
  • A four-year student-visa cap, a proposed $70,000-$100,000 fee for post-graduation work, and tighter green-card processing are squeezing the pipeline that feeds the H-1B program.

The H-1B program in 2026 is nearly unrecognizable. Over the past year the Trump administration has raised its cost, changed the lottery, proposed eliminating the grace period for laid-off workers and tightened enforcement - changes employers and lawyers say are reshaping who can work in America and at what price.

The seven challenges, explained

1. The $100,000 offshore fee. A September 2025 proclamation imposed a $100,000 payment on certain new H-1B petitions filed from abroad; an appeals court fast-tracked the legal challenge with arguments set for February 2026, just before the March cap season, according to Fast Company. IEEE Spectrum reported fee revenue fell $20 million as employers simply stopped filing.

2. The wage-weighted lottery. DHS scrapped the random cap lottery for wage-weighted selection effective February 27, 2026 - higher-paid candidates win, entry-level applicants lose.

3. The end of the grace period. A proposed rule published September 11 would kill the Obama-era 60-day grace period: laid-off H-1B, L-1, O-1 and TN workers would fall out of status the next day and risk deportation proceedings. It faces a 60-day comment period, USA Today reported.

4. Harsher enforcement. USCIS's "Catch-and-Revoke" policy cancels visas for any foreign national found to have violated any US law even once, the Hindu BusinessLine reported, while the Labor Department is scrutinizing IT staffing firms' H-1B hiring, per Bloomberg Tax.

5. The compliance burden. Approval rates held near 98%, but employers now face heavier documentation and vetting, shifting the program's real cost from approval to process, immigration attorney Kevin J. Andrews told The American Bazaar.

6. Green-card roadblocks. USCIS now requires permanent-residency applicants to return home during processing, Mint reported - a blow to H-1B holders on visa extensions. Separately proposed bills would demand $200,000-plus salaries and bar family reunification.

7. A shrinking pipeline. FY2026 registrations fell to 358,737 from over 480,000, the lowest since FY2022, per USCIS data reported by the Hindu BusinessLine. Tech layoffs, a four-year student-visa cap imposed in July, and a proposed $70,000-$100,000 charge for post-graduation work are thinning future applicants, IEEE Spectrum reported.

Context & Background

The H-1B lets US firms hire foreign workers in specialty occupations needing at least a bachelor's degree, capped at 85,000 a year; Indians are roughly three-fourths of holders, per Mint. DHS estimates nearly 66,000 workers a year lost, left or changed jobs from fiscal 2021 through 2025; about 3,800 a year had a new employer file a petition within the 60-day window - over 99% of them H-1B.

Impact & Analysis

Economists say the cost shock invites offshoring. "A lot of employers could swallow another hundred, or a thousand" in charges, "but $103,000 is a whole new ballgame," economist Madeline Zavodny told Bloomberg Tax. Sam Peak of the Economic Innovation Group said employers "have the means to offshore their operations in response when costs get too high." DHS's own analysis found no direct benefits for workers or employers - only lost wages and productivity.

"The H-1B approval rate for FY2025 is steady at about 98 percent, but the operating environment for FY2026 looks materially harder. The friction has moved from adjudication to architecture."

— Kevin J. Andrews, immigration attorney

Diaspora Angle

Indian professionals are the most exposed. With three-fourths of H-1B holders Indian, the offshore fee, wage-weighted lottery and possible end of the grace period directly hit Indian engineers, IT consultants and students on post-graduation work authorization - many now choosing between paying far more to stay or moving careers back to India.

What's Next

The fee rule's comment period runs through September 24, with court arguments in February 2026 and the March cap season soon after. The grace-period proposal faces its own 60-day comment period before DHS can finalize, change or abandon it. For now the 60-day window remains - but employers are already planning 2026 hiring as if H-1B access will stay expensive, wage-filtered and hard to secure.
